# Consensus for a Stateless Burn Pipeline: Full Design

## 0. Ground rules stated upfront

- **Fault model:** crash-stop workers, honest. No Byzantine tolerance (that would require signed records and 3f+1; noted at the end if you need it).
- **"No central brain" means:** no worker is privileged; every decision requires a quorum of independent workers. The durable substrate (Postgres/etcd/S3) provides *ordering and memory*, not *judgment* — it cannot invent a verdict. Without shared durable memory or reliable channels, multi-worker consensus under crashes is impossible (FLP); the substrate is the minimum assumption, not a brain.
- **Safety never depends on wall-clock time.** Timeouts appear only in liveness paths. This invariant is enforced by construction below.

---

## 1. What persists vs. what recomputes

### PERSISTS (durable, shared, authoritative — the *only* truth)

| Object | Form |
|---|---|
| Decision log | Hash-chained, append-only record sequence, totally ordered by substrate-assigned `seq` |
| Records | `GENESIS`, `HB`, `PROP`, `COMMIT`, `CP` (checkpoint), `ALARM` |
| Checkpoint blobs | Content-addressed, *derived*, verifiable, disposable — optimizations, never truth |

Nothing else. No worker owns durable state. A seat's **contributions** persist (its records are in the chain forever); its **state** does not.

### RECOMPUTES (per-spawn, per-loop, ephemeral)

| Object | How |
|---|---|
| Burned set | Fold over all `COMMIT` records |
| Frontier | Pure fold: union of all `children` in COMMIT verdicts − burned set. **Never stored directly** — it is a deterministic function of the commit stream |
| Pending proposals | `PROP` records within TTL window |
| Alive set | `HB` records within heartbeat window |
| Work selection | Pure function `(state, worker_id) → item` |
| Scouting results | Computed fresh; never cached durably |

---

## 2. The log — exact schema

```
record := {
  seq:   u64          // assigned by substrate (serial PK / etcd revision)
  writer: uuid
  type:  GENESIS|HB|PROP|COMMIT|CP|ALARM
  body:  bytes        // canonical encoding, per type below
  prev:  h256         // hash of record seq-1
  self:  h256 = H(seq ‖ writer ‖ type ‖ body ‖ prev)
}

GENESIS.body := { config_hash }         // code version + all parameters; workers
                                        // refuse logs whose config_hash ≠ theirs
HB.body      := { wall_ts, head_seq }   // liveness ONLY
PROP.body    := { item: h256, verdict_hash: h256, verdict: bytes }
COMMIT.body  := { items: [{item, verdict}], props: [u64...] }  // batched, ≤64 items
CP.body      := { base_seq, state_root: h256, blob_ref: h256 }
ALARM.body   := { reason, evidence_ref }
```

**Canonical encoding:** fixed field order, little-endian, length-prefixed, sorted maps. Verdict equality is **byte equality** after canonicalization — never semantic comparison. This is what makes "one voice" checkable mechanically.

**Substrate primitive required:** linearizable append-with-ordering. Concretely: Postgres `INSERT ... RETURNING seq` (trivially linearizable per statement); etcd revisioned put; or S3 conditional PUT on a head-pointer object. Pick Postgres or etcd for interactive tailing; S3 acceptable if commits are batched.

---

## 3. The worker loop (stateless, exact)

```text
on spawn:
  head     = read_head()
  cp       = latest_verifiable_checkpoint(≤ head)   # recompute state_root from own
                                                    # fold; mismatch ⇒ discard CP,
                                                    # extend replay
  state    = reduce(cp.state, log[cp.base_seq+1 .. head])
  my_id    = credential.uuid                        # from runtime, not from log

loop:
  if hb_due(): cas_append(HB{now, head})
  tail_read(); state = reduce(state, new_records)   # pure fold, byte-deterministic

  item = pick(state, my_id)
        # deterministic: max priority over (frontier − burned),
        # tie-break min item_id. Deliberately does NOT exclude items
        # under active proposal — redundancy is cheaper than the
        # extra consensus an exclusion lease would need.

  if item == ∅: sleep(poll); continue

  result  = scout(item)                             # the real work; no shared side effects
  v       = canon(render(result))
  cas_append(PROP{item, H(v), v})

  # commit path — ANY worker runs this, not just the proposer:
  P = { p ∈ state.props[item] : p.verdict_hash == H(v),
        distinct writers, (head.seq − p.seq) < TTL_RECORDS }
  if |P| ≥ ⌊N/2⌋+1  and  item ∉ state.burned:
      cas_append(COMMIT{items=[(item,v)], props=P})   # loser of CAS race sees the
                                                      # winner's COMMIT on re-read
                                                      # and treats it as success
```

**Reduce function (pure):**
```text
reduce(state, records):
  HB     → alive[writer] = wall_ts
  PROP   → if item ∉ burned: props[item][verdict_hash].add(record)
  COMMIT → burned ∪= items; enqueue(children in verdicts) minus burned;
           delete props[items]
```
Same prefix bytes ⇒ same state bytes, for every worker. Property-test this continuously.

---

## 4. Death and respawn — the exact contract

**Lost at death:**
- In-memory fold (rebuilt in milliseconds from checkpoint + tail).
- An un-appended in-flight scout result (item simply gets re-scouted by someone; scouting is idempotent).
- Local caches.

**Survives death:**
- Every record it ever got appended (`PROP`s included). A `PROP` that was already in the log is *not lost work* — other workers can complete its quorum from the recorded verdict bytes.
- Everything quorum-committed, anywhere, by anyone.

**Respawn procedure:** read head → verify chain hashes → load newest checkpoint whose `state_root` matches an independent recompute → fold tail → resume. Old `PROP`s from a previous incarnation are handled by the normal rules: still within TTL and matching ⇒ they count toward quorum; expired ⇒ ignored, item returns to the pickable pool.

**Cost bound:** checkpoint every 4096 records ⇒ replay is O(4096) small records + one blob fetch. Cold-start target: low hundreds of ms. Checkpoint writer = whoever's record lands at `seq % 4096 == 0`; it opportunistically appends `CP`. No coordination — a bad checkpoint fails verification and is discarded.

---

## 5. Why there is no drift — mechanism by mechanism

1. **Total order:** substrate-linearized log; all workers read the identical sequence.
2. **Pure reduce:** identical input bytes ⇒ identical state bytes; no hidden per-worker interpretation.
3. **Quorum-gated COMMIT:** no minority, no partition survivor, no single faulty writer can inject a fact. Minority side physically cannot burn; it stalls, then converges on heal.
4. **Hash chain:** any fork or corruption is detected; the honest response is `ALARM` + halt, never divergence.
5. **Byte-canonical verdicts:** "agreement" is byte equality, eliminating semantic-judgment drift.
6. **Consumers read COMMIT only:** the pipeline's external voice *is* the commit stream — singular by construction, independently auditable via chain hashes.
7. **Genesis config hash:** mixed-version fleets cannot silently interpret records differently.

**Races resolved by rule, not luck:**
- Two workers race to COMMIT the same item → CAS lets exactly one land; the loser re-reads, sees the COMMIT, moves on (idempotent outcome).
- Stale `PROP` (V₁) vs. committed V₂ → COMMIT beats any PROP regardless of order; the late V₁ PROP is a no-op.
- Conflicting verdicts, neither reaching quorum → both expire by TTL (measured in **record distance**, not seconds); item re-enters the pool.

---

## 6. Burning = exactly-once *effects*, not just decisions

Consensus protects the **decision**. The real-world burn effect needs its own guard:

- **Hard pipeline invariant: every burn effect is idempotent** (delete-by-key, upsert, payment with idempotency key). This is a requirement on effect design, not an option.
- The `COMMIT` record is the permission slip. Executors scan for COMMITs lacking an `EFFECT_DONE` marker, perform the effect with `idempotency_key = item_id`, append `EFFECT_DONE`. Concurrent executors converge because the effect itself is idempotent — no extra coordination.

---

## 7. Parameters

| Param | Value | Role |
|---|---|---|
| N | 3–9 | quorum overhead grows linearly; sweet spot |
| Quorum Q | ⌊N/2⌋+1 | safety |
| Heartbeat | 5 s; dead after 15 s | liveness only |
| PROP TTL | 64 records or 60 s | garbage-collect stalled proposals |
| Checkpoint | every 4096 records | bounds respawn replay |
| Commit batch | ≤64 items | amortizes quorum cost ~64× |
| Throughput ceiling | ~5–10k appends/s on plain Postgres ⇒ ~300–600k burns/s batched | before any sharding |

---

## 8. If you need Byzantine tolerance later

Add Ed25519 signatures on every record, raise quorum to 2f+1 of 3f+1, and make `prev` checks signature-aware. The architecture above is unchanged; only the admission math changes. Design so that retrofit touches the record envelope and quorum counter — nothing else.

---

**Summary in one line:** persist *only* the hash-chained quorum-committed decision stream; recompute *everything else* as a pure fold over it. A seat that dies loses nothing but milliseconds of folding, because its voice — once appended and ratified — is already part of the one honest voice.
reasoning:
Let me parse this problem carefully.

The user is asking about a "frontier-scout burn pipeline" — this sounds like a distributed system where N stateless workers need to reach consensus without a central coordinator ("no central brain"), speaking as "one honest voice, no drift." The key constraint: a stateless seat (worker) that dies and respawns. What persists vs. what recomputes?

This is a systems design question about:
1. Stateless workers achieving consensus
2. No central coordinator
3. Deterministic behavior across death/respawn cycles
4. A "burn pipeline" — likely meaning work items get consumed/burned as they're processed

Let me think about what "frontier-scout burn pipeline" means concretely:
- Frontier: the set of unexplored/unprocessed items (like frontier in graph search, or frontier in exploration)
- Scout: workers that probe the frontier
- Burn: consuming work items — once burned, they're done, never revisited

The core tension: stateless workers + consensus + no drift. If workers are truly stateless, all state must live somewhere external and shared. Consensus without a central brain means either:
1. Shared append-only log with deterministic reduction
2. Quorum-based agreement on each step
3. Deterministic total ordering via some external sequencer (but that's a central brain)
4. CRDT-style convergence

"No drift" is the key phrase — all workers must agree on the same view of the world at any point. Drift happens when workers have divergent views of what's been burned, what's next, etc.

Let me design this properly:

**Core insight**: For stateless workers to speak as one voice with no drift, you need exactly one source of truth that is:
- Append-only (so history is immutable)
- Externally consistent (so all workers see the same sequence)
- Deterministically reducible (so any worker can reconstruct full state from the log)

**What persists**:
1. The decision log / ledger — every burn decision, every frontier advance, every scout verdict
2. The epoch/generation counter — so respawned seats know which era they're in
3. Commitments/hashes — Merkle roots or content hashes so workers can verify they're on the same page without reading everything

**What recomputes**:
1. In-memory caches of derived state (frontier index, priority queues)
2. Any speculative work not yet committed to the log
3. Worker-local heuristics, scoring functions (these are pure functions of committed state)

**Consensus mechanism without central brain**:
Options:
a) **Deterministic leader election per round** — but leader election itself needs consensus... unless it's derived from the log deterministically (e.g., lowest worker ID alive, determined by heartbeat entries in the log). This is self-referential but works if heartbeats are logged.
b) **Quorum voting on each proposal** — Raft-like but without persistent leader state; each proposal gets voted on.
c) **Shared log with atomic append** — if there's an external storage system (S3, Redis, Postgres) that provides linearizable appends, that's your sequencer. But is that a "central brain"? It's infrastructure, not intelligence. I'd argue the "brain" is the logic; the log is just memory. But strictly, a single-writer lock is a central arbiter.
d) **Two-phase commit style with deterministic tie-breaking**

Actually, let me think harder. "No central brain" — the cleanest interpretation: no single worker has authority; decisions emerge from quorum or from deterministic rules applied to shared state. The shared state lives in durable storage (which persists), but no worker is special.

**Design sketch**:

Storage layer (persists):
- `log/` — append-only sequence of records, each with monotonic sequence number
- Each record: `{seq, epoch, proposer_id, type, payload, prev_hash}` — hash-chained for tamper evidence
- Types: `HEARTBEAT`, `PROPOSE_BURN(item_id, verdict)`, `COMMIT_BURN(item_id)`, `FRONTIER_ADVANCE(new_frontier_hash)`, `EPOCH_BOUNDARY`

Worker algorithm (stateless):
1. On spawn: read tail of log (last K records or since last checkpoint), rebuild in-memory view
2. Verify hash chain — if broken, halt and alert (honesty enforcement)
3. Loop:
   - Read current frontier view
   - Pick item(s) to scout (deterministic given view + worker ID for tie-break)
   - Do the actual scouting work (probe the frontier item)
   - Propose verdict: write `PROPOSE` record
   - Wait for quorum of PROPOSEs on same item with same verdict → anyone can write COMMIT
   - COMMIT makes it real; item is burned

Wait — but who writes COMMIT? If multiple workers try, we get duplicate commits. Need idempotency: COMMIT record includes the set of PROPOSE seqs it's based on; first valid COMMIT wins (checked via compare-and-swap on the log's expected next seq, or by checking no prior COMMIT exists for that item).

Hmm, this is getting into the weeds. Let me think about what storage primitive we assume. The problem says "no central brain" — I'll interpret: no worker is privileged, but there IS a shared durable substrate (otherwise nothing persists and the question "what persists vs recomputes" is meaningless). The substrate provides:
- Linearizable append (or CAS on a counter)
- Reads

That's fair — S3 conditional puts, DynamoDB transactions, etcd, Postgres, even a file with flock. The "brain" (decision logic) is distributed; the memory is shared.

**Drift prevention**:
Drift = two workers believing different things about burned items or frontier state. Sources of drift:
1. Reading stale log → fix: read with consistency token (e.g., read up to seq X, include X in proposals; commits validate against current head)
2. Divergent interpretation of same log → fix: deterministic reduction function, versioned schema
3. Split-brain during network partition → fix: quorum requirement (majority of known-alive workers); minority cannot commit
4. Non-deterministic worker logic → fix: pure functions only; any randomness seeded from log-derived entropy

**Death and respawn**:
A seat dies mid-scout. What's lost:
- Its in-flight proposal (uncommitted PROPOSE) — either expires (TTL) or gets superseded
- Its local cache of frontier state
- Its lease on any item it claimed

What survives:
- All COMMITted burns
- All PROPOSEs still within TTL window
- Epoch counter
- Hash chain

On respawn:
- Read log from last checkpoint (or full replay if no checkpoint)
- Rebuild view
- Detect its own old PROPOSEs — treat them as expired if past TTL, or re-affirm if still valid
- Resume

**Leases vs leases-free**: 
For the burn pipeline, do we need leases on items? If two scouts probe the same item simultaneously, that's wasted work but not incorrect — both propose, quorum dedupes. Leases add complexity and failure modes (expired lease held by dead worker). Better: leaseless, idempotent, redundant-tolerant. Cost: possible duplicate scouting work. Mitigation: deterministic work assignment (worker i takes items where hash(item) % N == i among alive set) — but "alive set" needs consensus too...

Alive set determination: heartbeats in the log. Worker writes HEARTBEAT every T seconds. Alive = heartbeat within 2T. But reading "alive set" requires reading recent log — fine. Membership changes cause reassignment churn; use rendezvous hashing keyed on (epoch, alive_set_hash) to minimize movement.

Actually, simpler: don't assign work exclusively. Every idle worker picks the highest-priority unburned, uncommitted item and scouts it. Duplicate scouting is acceptable overhead. Priority order is deterministic function of committed state. This eliminates the alive-set consensus problem entirely for work assignment. Only the commit path needs quorum.

**Quorum details**:
- N workers, majority Q = floor(N/2)+1 must PROPOSE identical verdict for an item before COMMIT
- Verdict identity: exact bytes of verdict payload (canonical serialization)
- COMMIT writer: any worker observing Q matching PROPOSEs may attempt COMMIT via CAS on log head; losers retry or move on
- Idempotency: COMMIT includes item_id; check no existing COMMIT for item_id in log index

But wait — how does a worker know the full log to check "no existing COMMIT for item_id"? Log could be huge. Need an index: either maintained incrementally (each worker builds map item_id→commit_seq during replay) or a separate compacted store. Since workers are stateless, they rebuild the index on spawn from checkpoint + tail. Checkpoints are themselves log records written periodically by whoever notices the checkpoint interval elapsed (deterministic trigger: when seq % K == 0, the proposer of that record also writes a CHECKPOINT record containing Merkle root + compacted state snapshot reference).

Hmm, checkpoints contain state snapshots — where do snapshots live? Same durable store, content-addressed. Writing a checkpoint is itself a consensus action? No — checkpoint is derived data, verifiable by hash. Anyone can verify a checkpoint against the log prefix it claims to summarize. If wrong, ignore and fall back to full replay. So checkpoints are optimizations, not truth. Truth = log only.

**Honesty / one honest voice**:
"One honest voice" — workers must not diverge in what they say. Enforcement:
- Hash-chained log: any fork visible immediately
- Canonical serialization: verdicts compared byte-exact after canonicalization
- Deterministic reduction: given same log prefix, all workers compute same state — property testable
- Quorum: no single worker can inject a divergent fact
- On detecting inconsistency (hash mismatch, invalid record): worker halts itself and writes ALARM record (or just halts; alarm optional)

Byzantine tolerance? The problem says "one honest voice" — I think this means honest-but-faulty (crash faults), not Byzantine. N workers, crash-stop, majority quorum gives safety. If Byzantine were needed, we'd need 3f+1 and signed records. I'll note the assumption: crash faults only; for Byzantine, add signatures and raise quorum to 2f+1 of 3f+1.

**Epoch handling**:
Epoch increments when membership changes? Or when a worker detects it missed records? Simpler: epoch = monotonically increasing counter in log, bumped by EPOCH_START record when a new worker joins (it writes JOIN record with its ID; epoch bumps if the alive-set changed). Actually epochs complicate things. Alternative: no explicit epochs; liveness via heartbeats, correctness via quorum. Respawned worker just replays and continues. Epoch only matters for deterministic work assignment, which we dropped. Drop epochs. Keep a `gen` counter only inside checkpoint records for debugging.

Hmm wait, but the question explicitly says "Design it for a stateless seat that dies and respawns: what persists vs recomputes." So the answer should be organized around persist-vs-recompute. Let me structure:

**PERSISTS (durable, shared, authoritative)**:
1. The hash-chained decision log (the only source of truth)
   - Records: HEARTBEAT, PROPOSE, COMMIT, CHECKPOINT, ALARM
   - Each: {seq, ts, writer_id, type, payload, prev_hash}
2. Content-addressed checkpoint blobs (derived, verifiable, disposable)
3. Nothing else. No worker-local durable state. No config in the log beyond bootstrap constants (N, quorum rule, TTLs — these are code constants, versioned by deployment; if changed, new log namespace).

**RECOMPUTES (per-spawn, per-loop, ephemeral)**:
1. Frontier view: replay log tail from latest verified checkpoint → build {burned_set index, pending_proposals, priorities}
2. Proposal index: item_id → list of (seq, verdict_hash, writer)
3. Alive set: heartbeats within window
4. Work selection: pure function(view, worker_id)
5. Scouting results: computed fresh each time; never cached durably (if expensive, cache keyed by (item_id, frontier_version) in memory only, invalidated on view change)
6. Verdicts: pure function of scouting result + committed context

**The loop, exactly**:

```
on spawn:
  head = read_log_head()                      # linearizable read
  cp = latest_valid_checkpoint(≤ head)        # verify merkle root against log prefix hash
  state = reduce(log[cp.seq+1 .. head], cp.state)
  my_id = credential.id                       # from runtime, not log
  
loop:
  send_heartbeat_if_due(state.head_seq)
  refresh state if head moved: state = reduce(new_records, state)
  
  item = pick_next_unburned(state)            # deterministic: max priority, tie-break by item_id
  if none: sleep(poll_interval); continue
  
  result = scout(item)                        # the actual work; side-effect-free w.r.t. shared state
  verdict = canon(render(result))             # canonical bytes
  
  cas_append(PROPOSE{item, verdict_hash, verdict})   # linearizable append; retry on conflict
  
  # commit path (any worker, including proposer):
  props = collect PROPOSEs for item with identical verdict_hash, distinct writers, within ttl
  if |props| ≥ Q and no COMMIT{item} in state:
    cas_append(COMMIT{item, verdict, prop_seqs})
    state.burned.add(item)
```

**CAS append**: the substrate must give us "append iff head == expected". With S3: conditional PUT on a versioned key holding the log head pointer + object per record. With Postgres: INSERT with serial PK, trivially linearizable. With files+flock: fine for small N. State the assumption plainly.

**Duplicate-commit race**: Two workers both see Q proposals and both attempt COMMIT. CAS ensures only one lands. Loser reads head, sees COMMIT already present, treats as success (idempotent outcome). 

**Stale-proposal hazard**: Worker A proposes verdict V1 at seq 100. Network stalls. Others propose V2, commit at seq 105. A wakes, tries to gather quorum for V1 — sees COMMIT for item with different verdict. Rule: COMMIT wins over any PROPOSE regardless of order; a PROPOSE for an already-COMMITted item is a no-op. Safety preserved because COMMIT required quorum of identical verdicts.

**Conflicting verdicts, neither quorum**: Both die out via TTL. Item returns to pickable pool. Scouting repeats. Liveness OK.

**TTL choice**: proposals expire after T_ttl > max expected scout duration + max clock skew allowance... actually avoid clock dependence: TTL measured in log-seq distance, not wall time. Proposal valid while (head_seq - prop_seq) < K_records. Deterministic, no clocks needed except heartbeats which... heartbeats need wall time. Hmm. Heartbeats: wall-clock based, but only affect liveness (work distribution), never safety. Fine — safety never depends on time; liveness uses timeouts. That's the standard split and worth stating.

**Partition behavior**: Minority side cannot reach quorum → cannot commit → cannot burn → pipeline pauses on that side. Majority continues. On heal, minority replays, converges. No drift because no minority-side facts ever enter the log.

**Respawn cost analysis**: 
- Replay from checkpoint: O(records since checkpoint + checkpoint load). Checkpoint every K=10k records → bounded.
- Cold start latency: dominated by checkpoint fetch + tail reduce. Target: < few hundred ms for K=10k small records.
- What a respawned seat must NOT trust: its own pre-death in-flight PROPOSE (may be expired/superseded — recheck against current head), any uncommitted scouting result (recompute or re-propose; cheap because scouting is idempotent).

**What about the "one voice" output?** Downstream consumers of the pipeline read COMMIT records only. They never read PROPOSEs. So externally, the pipeline speaks with one voice: the committed stream. Consumers can verify the chain hash. That's the "one honest voice": the COMMIT stream, hash-chained, quorum-backed.

**Failure of the substrate?** Out of scope-ish but state it: substrate durability is the persistence assumption; if substrate loses data, everything is lost — mitigate with cross-region replication of the log bucket/table, which the substrate provides.

**Numbers/concretes**:
- Record size: ~200–800 bytes typical
- Heartbeat interval: 5s; considered dead after 15s (3 misses)
- Proposal TTL: 64 records or 60s, whichever first
- Checkpoint every 4096 records
- Quorum: ⌊N/2⌋+1
- N sizing: 3–9 workers sweet spot; quorum overhead grows linearly

**Schema, exact**:

```
record := {
  seq: u64,              // assigned by substrate CAS
  writer: uuid,
  type: enum {HB, PROP, COMMIT, CP, ALARM},
  body: bytes,           // canonical-encoded per type
  prev: h256,            // hash of record seq-1
  self: h256 = H(seq||writer||type||body||prev)
}

PROP.body  := { item: h256, verdict_hash: h256, verdict: bytes }
COMMIT.body:= { item: h256, verdict: bytes, props: [u64] }   // props = supporting PROP seqs
CP.body    := { base_seq: u64, state_root: h256, blob_ref: h256 }
HB.body    := { wall_ts: u64, head_seq: u64 }
```

Canonical encoding: fixed field order, little-endian, length-prefixed strings, sorted maps. Byte-exact comparison for verdict equality.

**State reduction function** (pure):

```
reduce(state, records):
  for r in records:
    case HB:    alive[r.writer] = r.body.wall_ts
    case PROP:  if r.body.item ∉ burned: props[r.body.item][r.body.verdict_hash].add(r)
    case COMMIT: burned.add(r.body.item); del props[r.body.item]; last_commit=r.seq
    case CP:    (optional fast-forward if trusted & verified)
  return state
```

All workers running same reduce on same prefix → identical state. Testable property: property-based test asserting reduce(prefix) == reduce(prefix') whenever prefix ≡ prefix'.

**Pick function** (pure):

```
pick(state, my_id):
  candidates = frontier_items - burned - (items with fresh quorum-in-progress?) 
  # deliberately do NOT exclude items under active proposal: redundancy is fine, exclusion needs extra consensus
  return argmax(priority, tie-break min item_id)
```

Optionally stagger: skip if (hash(item) % len(alive)) != index(my_id in alive) — reduces duplicate scouting ~N× but couples to alive-set churn. Offer as tunable, default off for small N where duplicate cost < coordination cost.

**Why no drift, precisely**:
1. Single totally ordered log (substrate-linearized) — everyone reads the same sequence
2. Pure deterministic reduce — same input bytes → same state bytes
3. Quorum-gated COMMIT — no minority/faulty writer can inject divergence
4. Hash chain — forks/corruption detected, halting rather than diverging
5. Canonical bytes — "same verdict" is byte equality, not semantic judgment
6. Consumers read only COMMIT — external voice is singular by construction

**Liveness risks** (be honest):
- Substrate CAS contention under high throughput → shard log by pipeline stage if needed; or batch
- Scout work non-idempotent in effect (e.g., burning sends an email) → then COMMIT must gate the *effect*, not just record it: effect executor runs post-commit, keyed by item_id, exactly-once via commit-record-as-dedup-token. Important nuance! The "burn" side effect must happen exactly once, driven by COMMIT, executed by whoever observes the COMMIT first, guarded by idempotency key = item_id (+commit seq).
- Actually this deserves emphasis: the pipeline's purpose is to burn (consume) frontier items with real-world effects. The consensus protects the *decision*; the *execution* needs its own exactly-once guard. Pattern: COMMIT record is the permission slip; executor scans for COMMITs lacking EFFECT-DONE marker; writes EFFECT-DONE record after performing effect; concurrent executors for same item resolved by... hmm, this reintroduces coordination. Simplest: effects are naturally idempotent (upserts, deletes-by-key, payments with idempotency keys). Require effect idempotency as a pipeline invariant. State it as a hard requirement.

**Bootstrap**: First ever record: GENESIS with config hash (code version, params). Workers refuse to operate on logs whose genesis config-hash ≠ their binary's expected hash. Prevents mixed-version drift.

**Upgrades**: New code version → new genesis → new log namespace; drain old pipeline first. Or in-place with dual-read transition. Keep simple: version-gate at genesis.

Now — format. The user wants concrete, exact, grounded, no fluff. This is a deep technical design question. It deserves a thorough response with structure: headers, schemas, pseudocode, numbers. Markdown appropriate (this will be rendered presumably). Length: substantial but tight — every sentence earning its place. I'll organize:

1. Model & assumptions (what "no central brain" means here; fault model)
2. The one thing that persists: the log (schema)
3. Everything else recomputes (the reduce)
4. The worker loop (pseudocode)
5. Death & respawn protocol (exact steps, costs)
6. Why no drift (mechanism-by-mechanism)
7. Exactly-once burning (effects)
8. Parameters table
9. Failure modes & answers

One more consideration on "consensus without a central brain": someone might object the linearizable substrate IS a central brain. Address head-on: the substrate provides ordering (memory), not decisions (judgment). Decisions require quorum of independent workers; the substrate cannot invent a verdict. If even shared storage is disallowed, the problem is unsolvable for N>1 under crashes (FLP/impossibility of consensus without shared assumptions) — say that plainly: you need either shared durable memory or reliable channels; pick the substrate, it's not a brain.

Also address: why not leader election? Because leader = central brain + failover complexity + drift windows during failover. Quorum-per-decision is slower per op but has zero failover and zero drift windows. For a burn pipeline (decisions are small, throughput moderate), quorum-per-burn is right. If throughput demands, batch: one COMMIT covers a batch of items, amortizing quorum cost. Mention batching.

Batching detail: COMMIT.body.items = [item...], all with gathered quorum props. Batch size B=64. Reduces log writes ~B×.

Also: what does "scout" produce? A verdict like {reachable: bool, cost: f64, children: [ids]}. Frontier advance: burning an item may add children to frontier. Children enter frontier via the COMMIT record itself (verdict contains children) — so frontier growth is part of the committed verdict, no separate FRONTIER_ADVANCE record needed. Good simplification: COMMIT = burn + enqueue(children). Frontier = derived set: all children ever committed − all burned. Recomputed on spawn from log. Persisted implicitly in COMMIT records. 

So the frontier is never stored directly — it's a pure fold over COMMIT records. That's elegant and worth highlighting: persisted = decisions; derived = frontier. The frontier can always be rebuilt exactly because it's a deterministic function of the commit stream.

Priority function: pure function of item content + depth + committed stats. Versioned by genesis config hash.

Edge: duplicate children (two parents yield same child) → dedupe by item_id in reduce; child enqueued once (first commit wins by seq order). Deterministic.

Edge: cycle (child == ancestor) → burned-set check prevents reprocessing; item already burned → skip enqueue. Deterministic.

Termination: frontier drains when pick returns none and no pending props → workers idle-poll. Pipeline complete marker: optional DONE record when a worker observes empty frontier + empty props + quorum... eh, keep simple: DONE is advisory, written by any worker observing drained state twice across one heartbeat interval. Not critical path.

Respawn exactness — enumerate what a dead seat loses vs keeps:

LOST (recompute):
- in-memory state fold (ms-scale)
- in-flight PROP not yet appended (work lost; item re-scouted by someone)
- PROP appended but uncommitted (survives in log until TTL; others may finish it — actually good: work isn't lost, verdict bytes are in the log)
- local caches

KEPT (persist):
- its appended PROP/COMMIT/HB records (forever, hash-chained)
- anything committed by quorum involving its proposals

Key subtlety worth stating: a stateless seat's *contributions* persist even though its *state* doesn't. Identity (uuid) persists in records; the seat itself holds nothing.

Credential/identity on respawn: same uuid or new? If uuid comes from runtime credential, respawn may get new uuid → its old uncommitted PROPs orphan until TTL. Acceptable. If uuid stable (pinned credential), old PROPs remain attributable. Either works; recommend stable uuid for auditability, but correctness doesn't depend on it.

Clock usage audit: wall time appears ONLY in HB (liveness) and record timestamps (debugging). Safety paths (quorum, chain validity, reduce, pick) are time-free. State this invariant explicitly — it's the kind of thing that kills systems silently.

Substrate options with exact primitives:
- Postgres: `INSERT INTO log(writer,type,body,prev) VALUES (...) RETURNING seq` — serial gives total order; prev checked in txn. Linearizable per-statement.
- DynamoDB: transactional write on counter item + append item.
- S3: head-pointer object with conditional PUT (If-Match version), record objects content-addressed. Higher latency (~tens of ms), fine for batched commits.
- etcd: revision-numbered puts, natural fit, watch for tailing.

Tail reads: workers poll head pointer (or etcd watch / PG LISTEN-NOTIFY / S3 inventory lag — S3 worst for tailing; prefer PG/etcd for interactive, S3 for archival tier).

Throughput estimate: PG single-writer inserts ~5–10k/s trivially; batched commits ×64 items → ~300–600k burns/s ceiling before sharding. Plenty for a scout pipeline.

Checkpoint verification: CP record stores state_root = Merkle root over (burned set hash, props map hash, frontier digest). Verifier recomputes root from its own fold at base_seq; mismatch → discard CP, extend replay. CP blobs content-addressed by state_root. Writers of CP: the worker whose PROP landed at seq % 4096 == 0 opportunistically writes CP after computing fold — free rider, no coordination.

Alarm path: on chain break or reduce exception → worker writes ALARM (best effort) and exits nonzero. Orchestrator counts ALARMs; ≥ threshold → freeze pipeline (stop committing) pending human. Honest-voice guarantee includes refusing to speak when unsure.
